articles.title: Why repairability scores are showing up on more product pages
articles.subtitle: A niche spec sheet line item is becoming a marketing feature
articles.excerpt: Repairability scores used to be a niche detail buried in teardown reports. Now they're showing up directly on product pages.
articles.author: admin

content.text: Repairability used to be something you had to dig for, buried in a teardown report from a specialist site. It's increasingly showing up directly on manufacturer product pages instead, right next to battery capacity and screen size.
Regulation and demand, together

New right-to-repair rules in several regions require disclosure of repairability ratings, and manufacturers that score well have started using the number as a selling point rather than treating it as a compliance footnote.
Whether the scores meaningfully change purchasing decisions is still debated, but they've clearly changed how products get marketed.

articles.title: The browser extension store problem nobody wants to fix
articles.subtitle: Abandoned extensions with broad permissions are still live by the thousands
articles.excerpt: Thousands of browser extensions with broad data permissions are still listed and installable years after their developers stopped maintaining them.
articles.author: ashraf

content.text: A recent audit of extension stores found thousands of listings that haven't been updated in over three years, many still holding broad permissions to read and modify site content, despite appearing abandoned by their original developers.
Why cleanup is harder than it sounds

Removing an extension outright can break active users who still rely on it, so platform operators have generally favored warning labels over removal, a compromise that leaves the underlying risk in place.
Security researchers argue that permission scope, not developer activity, should be the primary trigger for review.

articles.title: USB-C finally became the universal standard it promised to be
articles.subtitle: It took a regulation to get the whole industry on the same page
articles.excerpt: After a decade of "universal" ports that weren't really universal, USB-C has finally reached the consistency it was always supposed to deliver.
articles.author: admin

content.text: USB-C has technically existed for close to a decade, but "technically USB-C" covered an enormous range of actual capability, from basic charging to full external displays, all using the same-looking connector.
What actually changed
Regulatory pressure, rather than voluntary industry alignment, is what finally forced manufacturers to standardize on a consistent minimum feature set behind the same port.
Accessory makers say returns related to cable and charger compatibility have dropped noticeably since the stricter labeling requirements took effect.

articles.title: Inside the last mechanical keyboard factory in town
articles.subtitle: A visit to where clicky switches are still hand-assembled
articles.excerpt: As most manufacturing moved overseas decades ago, this workshop kept building keyboards the old way, one switch at a time.
articles.author: ashraf

content.text: Overview
As most manufacturing moved overseas decades ago, this workshop kept building keyboards the old way, one switch at a time.
The details

A visit to where clicky switches are still hand-assembled. As most manufacturing moved overseas decades ago, this workshop kept building keyboards the old way, and today it's one of fewer than a handful left doing so at this scale.

Each switch passes through fourteen separate hands before it reaches a finished board, a process that takes roughly nine times longer than fully automated production but yields a defect rate the owners say is close to zero.
Why it still works
Demand from enthusiast buyers willing to pay a premium for hand-built quality has kept the workshop afloat even as larger competitors automated or closed entirely.
Our take

It's an encouraging sign for where the category is headed next, even if not every question has been answered yet — succession planning for a business this specialized remains an open question for the family that runs it.

articles.title: Why everyone is suddenly talking about on-device AI
articles.subtitle: It's not just a marketing buzzword anymore
articles.excerpt: Chipmakers and app developers are racing to move AI processing off the cloud and onto your pocket, and the reasons go beyond privacy.
articles.author: admin

content.text: Overview
Chipmakers and app developers are racing to move AI processing off the cloud and onto your pocket, and the reasons go beyond privacy.
The details

It's not just a marketing buzzword anymore. Chipmakers and app developers are racing to move AI processing off the cloud and onto your pocket, and the reasons go beyond privacy — running locally cuts response times from roughly 800 milliseconds to under 100.

Cost is the other driver: cloud inference at scale is expensive, and offloading even a third of requests to on-device hardware can meaningfully reduce a company's server bill, which explains why so many are investing here at once.
The tradeoffs

On-device models are still smaller and less capable than their cloud counterparts, so most apps use a hybrid approach: simple tasks run locally, while anything more complex still gets routed to a server.
The phone in your pocket is quietly becoming a small data center.
Our take
It's an encouraging sign for where the category is headed next, even if not every question has been answered yet — battery impact during sustained on-device use is still the biggest open question.
